entities.summary:
Giuseppe Archinto (1651–1712) was a prominent Italian diplomat and high-ranking prelate of the Roman Catholic Church, whose career spanned the late 17th and early 18th centuries, a period marked by intense geopolitical shifts in Europe. Born into the influential Archinto family of Milan, his trajectory from papal nuncio in critical European courts to Cardinal and Archbishop of Milan positioned him at the nexus of ecclesiastical authority and international diplomacy. Archinto's significance lies in his adept navigation of complex political landscapes, particularly his instrumental role in brokering the Treaty of Karlowitz, a landmark agreement that reshaped the balance of power between the Habsburg Empire and the Ottoman Porte.

His diplomatic career began with a nunciature in Florence (1686–1689), followed by a crucial assignment as Nuncio to Poland (1689–1695). During his Polish tenure, Archinto played a pivotal part in the negotiations that culminated in the Treaty of Karlowitz in January 1699. This treaty formally ended the Great Turkish War, ceding vast territories from the Ottoman Empire to the Habsburgs, Poland-Lithuania, and Venice. His contributions earned him the cardinalate from Pope Innocent XII in April 1699, shortly before his appointment as Archbishop of Milan, a position he held until his death. As archbishop, he focused on ecclesiastical reform and pastoral care within his archdiocese, particularly during the turbulent War of the Spanish Succession when Milanese territories were frequently contested.

His career exemplifies the significant political influence wielded by high-ranking Church officials in early modern diplomacy.
